title: The Magdeburg hemispheres
hook: Two teams of horses could not pull apart two bowls held together by air.
peek: In the 1650s Otto von Guericke pumped the air out of two copper half-spheres. With nothing inside, the outside air held them shut so hard that teams of horses could not separate them. Open a valve and they fell apart by hand.
lede: Otto von Guericke was the mayor of Magdeburg in Germany and a keen experimenter. Around 1650 he built one of the first air pumps. He fitted two copper half-spheres together with a greased rim and pumped out the air between them. Nothing held them shut except the air outside, yet teams of horses pulling in opposite directions could not drag them apart.

bullets.text: Guericke showed the trick in 1654 before Emperor Ferdinand III at the Imperial Diet in Regensburg, and again in Magdeburg. Accounts of the number of horses vary; the famous engraving shows two teams of eight.

Nothing inside was sucking. The air around us presses on every surface, about a kilogram on each square centimetre. With the air inside removed, there was nothing to push back, and that pressure clamped the halves together.
Once the horses gave up, Guericke opened a small valve. Air hissed back in, the pressure inside matched the outside, and the hemispheres simply came apart in his hands.
The second team of horses was showmanship. Tying one half to a post would have pulled just as hard, since the post pushes back as firmly as a second team. Guericke wanted a spectacle, and got one.
